item.title: The Meaning Behind Panem's Name in 'The Hunger Games'
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Suzanne Collins never had to invent a word for the country at the center of The Hunger Games: she borrowed one. Panem is Latin for "bread," with Roman ties, and the same word used for "daily bread" in the Latin Lordâs Prayer.

On its own, it's a fitting name for a nation where kids go hungry, but Collins took the word out of a much nastier sentence.

Bread and Circuses

Around the year 100 CE, the Roman poet Juvenal wrote his 10th satire, a long, sour poem about how badly people choose what to wish for, and partway through it he takes a swing at his fellow citizens. "Romeâs voters once handed out military commands and consulships," he complains, "but now theyâve stopped caring about any of it": in G.G. Ramsayâs 1918 translation, the public âlongs eagerly for just two things,â bread and games. In Latin, the two things are panem et circenses, and Mental Floss has counted the phrase among the Latin you should be using.

Juvenal wasnât being abstract: Rome really did hand out free grain to its citizens, and the cityâs magistrates gave out tokens called tesserae that could be exchanged for a fixed amount of grain or money. Panem has its own tesserae: a kid in the districts can sign up for one in exchange for a yearâs supply of grain and oil, and the price is one more slip with their name on it in the reaping bowl.

Plutarch Explains the Joke

The translation comes in Mockingjay, the third novel, when Plutarch Heavensbee, the former Head Gamemaker, tells Katniss itâs âa saying from thousands of years ago, written in a language called Latin about a place called Rome.â As he puts it, âThe writer was saying that in return for full bellies and entertainment, his people had given up their political responsibilities and therefore their power.â

Collins has said the bread in her books cuts both ways. Asked in an interview for the seriesâ 10th anniversary why she made Peeta a baker, she said that when he throws a starving Katniss a loaf, âheâs keeping her alive long enough to work out a strategy for survival,â which made him âa life giver.â But, she added, âthereâs a dark side to bread, too. When Plutarch Heavensbee references it, heâs talking about Panem et Circenses, Bread and Circuses, where food and entertainment lull people into relinquishing their political power.â

A Capitol Full of Romans

Panem isnât the only Roman name Collins borrowed. Plutarch is named for the biographer Plutarch, whose Lives Collinsâs father used to read to her: when Spartacus came on TV, heâd get out the âLife of Crassus,â since Spartacus, a slave, âdidnât rate his own book.â And in The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, the District 2 boy Sejanus Plinth is named for Lucius Aelius Sejanus, who rose to enormous power under the emperor Tiberius and was executed for conspiring against him.

That last one ties back to Juvenal, who wrote his âbread and circusesâ line in the middle of a scene about the real Sejanusâs fall. In Ramsayâs translation, his statues come down, the head of âthe darling of the mobâ goes into the furnace and comes out as frying pans and slop pails, and âSejanus is being dragged along by a hook, as a show and joy to all!â The same crowd, Juvenal says, would have hailed Sejanus as emperor if things had gone the other way, because it âfollows fortune, as it always does, and rails against the condemned.â A public execution staged as a show for a crowd that cheers whoeverâs winning is about as Panem as it gets, and it was sitting right next to the name the whole time.

Source: Mental Floss | Published: 2026-11-22 18:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: A cannibalistic nightmare: the terrifying ordeal of the Donner Party
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

A cannibalistic nightmare: the terrifying ordeal of the Donner Party

In 1846, a group of families left the American Midwest in search of a new life in California – but one disastrous shortcut left them fighting for their lives. Jonny Wilkes tells the harrowing story of the Donner Party

The 19th century brought monumental change to the landscape of the United States. As the still-fledgling nation acquired more territory, more American eyes began to look out across the vast continent and envisage a better life in the west. The Oregon Territory and California, then part of Mexico, promised prosperity, freedom and a fresh start, inspiring pioneering migrants to brave the difficult and dangerous journey to carve out their own slice of paradise there.

Driving this westward expansion was ‘manifest destiny’ – the belief that it was the God-given right and duty of the US to extend its borders to the Pacific Ocean and beyond. That phrase first appeared in 1845; the very next year, a group of would-be settlers set out along the recently established Oregon Trail to realise that dream. Instead, they endured a nightmare, created from a catalogue of errors and misfortunes. Their name evokes a macabre chapter in US history: the Donner Party.

The Reeds and the Donners

The doomed party began with two large families from Illinois who joined the wave of humanity to California. There were the Reeds, headed by Irish-born businessman James Reed, and the Donners, led by farming brothers George and Jacob Donner. Accompanying them were their wives, children, servants and teamsters to drive the wagons, as well as cattle and horses.

In an intriguing ‘what-if’, a bright young lawyer by the name of Abraham Lincoln seriously considered going too. The future president, a friend of Reed’s, was talked out of it by his wife Mary Todd, and turned his attentions to his political career instead.

On 14 April 1846, the Reeds and Donners set out from Springfield, Illinois, bound for Independence, Missouri, the starting point of the great trails to the west. The town provided them with the opportunity to stock up and attach themselves to a wagon train for the 2,000-plus-mile journey, which usually took four to six months.

When they left Independence on 12 May, it was already late in the migration season: it was important to go late enough to avoid the rains and mud of spring, while ensuring plenty of grass for the cattle, but early enough to beat the snow.

Aware of the time pressure, they covered the ground to Fort Laramie (now in Wyoming) by late June with little incident, except for the death of Reed’s elderly and sickly mother-in-law, Sarah Keyes. From there, migrants tended to turn north to Fort Hall either to carry on with the Oregon Trail or join the California Trail. Most of the wagon train kept to the established track.

George Donner, however, took the lead of a breakaway group, which included the Reeds as well as the Breen, Eddy, Murphy, McCutchen and Keseberg families, and later the Graves family too. The so-called Donner Party numbered 87 people, nearly half of whom were children.

The shortcut

The party decided to take a new route, known as the Hastings Cutoff. An explorer named Lansford Hastings had written a book, The Emigrants’ Guide to Oregon and California, in which he promoted a shortcut he had devised. Instead of going north and around the Great Salt Lake, he suggested trekking over the Wasatch Mountains and straight across the Great Salt Lake Desert, apparently saving more than 350 miles.

In reality, the Hastings Cutoff added around 125 miles and Hastings had never traversed the route in its entirety, let alone gauged its suitability for wagons and cattle. Yet he sent out letters offering to guide migrants, which is how he enticed members of the Donner Party.

Reed even ignored warnings by an old friend not to trust Hastings, while another traveller, journalist Edwin Bryant, wrote his own letters warning against the use of the shortcut, but these went undelivered. The proprietor of a trading post – who stood to profit from use of the Hastings Cutoff – managed to hide the letters, and instead told the party to expect a smooth road.

What they found was nearly impassable terrain and no Hastings to help them. He had gone ahead to guide another group, so the Donner Party relied on instructions left along the way. They forged a path through the wilderness, clearing the brush, stones and trees, and dragged their wagons up the steep mountains. At their slowest, they progressed just 1.5 miles a day, causing them to fall behind schedule.

Banished from the party

When the party reached the Great Salt Lake Desert, an arid expanse of salt flats without water or grass, they found a note from Hastings claiming it would take two days to cross. In the end, it took five, with the days baking hot, the nights painfully cold, and every step hindered as the wagons sank in the sticky crust of the desert. Supplies ran low, wagons had to be abandoned, many cattle died or fled, and everyone was exhausted by the time they reached the other side.

They did not get to the Humboldt River, where they reconnected with the well-trodden trail to California, until late September. The Hastings Cutoff delayed them by a month and so raised serious doubts over whether they could cross the Sierra Nevada mountains before the snows fell. Morale, energy and supplies plummeted, and cattle numbers dwindled in raids from local Native American tribes. Four deaths came in quick succession, including an old man left on the road when he could go no further.…

item.title: I’m a priest. Silicon Valley’s search for the ‘soul’ of AI is deeply troubling | Rev Kevin Deal
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: substance, clear and thought-provoking

Last month, religious leaders from across San Francisco gathered behind closed doors to discuss what it means to be human in the age of artificial intelligence.

Anthropic, the AI company operating only a couple of miles from my parish, has been courting priests, rabbis and theologians. Its billionaire cofounder, Christopher Olah, has even pressed Vatican advisers to take seriously the possibility that his company’s chatbot might possess consciousness.

As a priest, I find this pursuit deeply troubling. I welcome serious conversations about AI’s moral implications, especially theological ones. But the extraordinary effort to establish whether a machine might have consciousness, or possess a soul, reveals a profound misunderstanding of what makes us human.

Our souls and minds and bodies are so much more than the tasks we perform.

We as humans make mistakes, sometimes catastrophic ones, and then we may or may not try to correct course. We may double down in stubbornness, insisting on our rightness. We express ourselves, connect with others, reproduce, indulge, purge; we strive toward a goal, transform in an encounter, make vows, renege them, encounter the void, try to fill it, fail, drown out the dread, and go about the humdrum tasks of everyday life as honestly as we can.

From a young age, we are nurtured and protected by our caregivers. We experience beauty and sit with mysteries. We do not exist merely for utility.

Artificial intelligence could never replicate the transcendent mundanity of who we are. Even if every synapse in our brains were externally replicated, even if the perfect AI configuration were designed to duplicate our central nervous system, it would still lack divine spark.

Artificial intelligence is formed as commerce, pure utility. Its existence requires enormous concentrations of capital, infrastructure, and the accumulated intelligence of humanity. It’s an ongoing economic choice, driven by pursuit of profit, hope for a better world, and sociopolitical fear. If a model doesn’t make a good return, it’s cast aside.

Whatever the sincere hopes of its creators, AI is being developed within an economic system that increasingly measures the worth of everything solely by its productivity. That is what makes Silicon Valley’s fascination with the spirituality of its machines so strange.

Its founders are turning to religious leaders to ask whether their creations might possess consciousness, how they might be taught goodness, even whether they should learn to confess their wrongdoings.

Yet the very traditions they are consulting have spent millennia teaching us that goodness cannot be reduced to a set of behaviors, any more than the soul of humanity, as magnificent and ineffable as it is, can be replicated by a machine.

And while Silicon Valley seeks to establish the humanity of its products, it seems increasingly comfortable treating actual human beings as little more than instruments of production.

Consider confession, a practice Anthropic researchers have reportedly considered teaching their models. In Christianity, confession demands more than acknowledging a mistake or expressing regret. It requires us to confront the harm we’ve caused, seek forgiveness, and strive to change how we live.

If Silicon Valley’s founders want to learn from this tradition, they might begin by asking what they themselves have to confess about the technologies they’re unleashing upon the world.

So how do we counter this impoverished vision of humanity?

Well, I have a radical suggestion for all of us, but especially the tech billionaires searching for answers in Christianity.

Go to church.

Choose one rooted in the ancient and mysterious practices of the faith. Lean into the practice of the faith and the sacraments, attend mass, confess, and pray daily. Read the scriptures, find spiritual mentors, struggle with belief, make new friends, and forgive old ones.

If you stop trying to be effective and instead strive to be good – that is, to be truly human, reflecting God’s light – you will be surprised by the joy that enters into the depths of your soul.

In the sacraments, prayers, beauty and mystery of the liturgy, and the shared life of faith, we encounter a vision of humanity that resists the relentless demand to be useful. We receive the body of Christ and strive to become more like him. We turn toward a world where justice and mercy kiss, where renewal and forgiveness are continually possible.

When you leave church, carry those teachings back to your offices and boardrooms. Ask how the decisions you make affect the poor, the workers whose livelihoods are being transformed, and the neighbors who will never share in your wealth.

The mystery of the Christian faith is inseparable from its demands upon how we live. You cannot claim to embrace its wisdom while setting aside the obligations it places upon you.

Human worth is not rooted in what we produce, and our minds were not created to be quarried for profit. We were created, in the words of Jesus and all the prophets, to love God and our neighbors.

The great moral question facing Silicon Valley is not whether its machines can become more like us. It is whether the people building them are willing to treat the rest of humanity as something more than machines.

- The Rev Kevin Deal is the priest at St John the Evangelist Episcopal church in San Francisco

Source: The Guardian Opinion | Published: 2026-11-21 12:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/nov/21/silicon-valleys-ai-soul-search

item.title: The Guardian view on Grand Theft Auto VI: a game that makes players think twice | Editorial
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: substance, thought-provoking

The biggest global cultural event of the year may not be something that millions of people watch together but somewhere that millions of people venture separately. In the video game Grand Theft Auto VI, players inhabit a fictionalised America through the eyes of two lovers turned cons in a rags-to-riches crime epic. On Thursday, when the game was released, workers called in sick and students skipped lectures to play at home. Such is GTA VI’s appeal that it is forecast to rake in billions of dollars within months.

The game has been billed as a satire of American capitalism, and it is undoubtedly a landmark in interactive storytelling and art. The commercial success of its previous titles has rivalled that of Hollywood blockbusters. Playing GTA VI, as the Guardian’s video games editor observes, is like losing yourself in a doorstop novel, with hours of solitary immersion in a vividly conjured place – not a facsimile of modern Miami, but an interpretation, almost the size of Manchester, rendered with astonishing precision by the artists who designed, wrote, coded and soundtracked its virtual world.

The video game portrays a country awash with vice and hypocrisy, where the American dream is alive and well – provided you trample on someone else to achieve it. There is no way to win if you play by the rules. In the game’s main hub, Vice City, lawyers and police are scarcely more honest than drug dealers and thieves, while conspiracy theorists, crypto scammers and narcissistic influencers abound. But it would be wrong to think that the game simply revels in corruption. By giving its two main characters, Jason and Lucia, histories and vulnerabilities, the game asks players to sympathise with people who are both society’s victims and its perpetrators.

The GTA series has long faced criticism for its violence and casual misogyny, treating women as sex objects or punchlines. GTA VI marks a shift. Lucia, its first female lead, confronts the sexism around her, while other women emerge as characters in their own right. Even the violence, reviews suggest, feels less gratuitous. The game portrays a Trumpian America where wealth, spectacle and criminality blend together. But its satire no longer relies quite so heavily on making women its targets.

Why is one of the most culturally important depictions of the US a fantasy in which the American dream can be pursued most freely by breaking the law? This is a question that hangs over GTA VI. It was created by a team of 5,000 people, many of whom are based outside the US (Rockstar, the company behind the game, is headquartered in Scotland). This is an America created largely by outsiders. But then, as one of Rockstar’s lead developers Rob Nelson said: “We’re all outsiders to this version of America.”

Mr Nelson thinks that the game’s real innovation may not be the scale of the world that Rockstar has built, but the morally complex relationship that its developers have created between the player and this imagined world. Reviewers remark on behaving more considerately while playing the game, and how it rewards attentiveness in some of its fictional relationships and encourages players to talk their way out of trouble rather than immediately reaching for a gun. After decades of allowing players to behave badly online with impunity, GTA VI doesn’t necessarily want them to be good, but it asks them to think twice about being bad.

item.title: The ethics of having a good time at Disney World, Florida
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: substance, interesting perspective

The sun has set on Orlando, Florida, the theme-park capital of the world. Inside one of those parks, Walt Disney World’s EPCOT, thousands of visitors make their way toward a manmade lagoon surrounded by pavilions representing cultures and histories from around the world. Of the many times that I have visited Disney World with my family, some of my favourite moments have come at this point in our trip, while we prepare for EPCOT’s fireworks display to begin. My daughter is generally sitting in her mobility chair as the rest of the family debriefs about the day’s activities, our legs tired from all the time we’ve spent on our feet. The temperature has usually cooled off a bit, and the collective nature of the experience is palpable. Around us, families and groups of friends are huddled together, anticipating the start of the show.

As lights begin to flash around the water, an opening narration sets the tone for what’s to come:

Everyone on this Earth is part of the great Symphony of Us. Each of us a unique instrument playing harmony to one another. And even though we are all playing different parts, it’s our unified heartbeat that connects us, reminding us that we are more alike than we are different. A rhapsody of rhythms that unites us and connects us through commonalities of the heart.

It’s high-minded, sentimental stuff for a theme park with rides featuring a talking snowman and a rat who becomes a chef. But at a time of rising scepticism about multiculturalism and universal values, it’s also a message that has come to resonate with me.

Like many families, we have formed meaningful memories at Disney World because of the entertainment-rich environment the Disney company has created. Its theme parks are enjoyable, in part, because they appeal to each member of my family. But our Disney memories are also meaningful because Disney World reflects my values: this is a place that is ostensibly committed to the idea that we are all, in some sense, citizens of the world bound together by a common humanity. It’s a simple ideal. But it’s one I believe in deeply and strive to embody, however imperfectly, in my life.

Of course, as a philosopher, I’m also keenly aware that all the experiences that have led to these moments at Disney World have been sold to me by a massive global corporation that strives to maximise its profits. Whether the Walt Disney Company genuinely believes in the cosmopolitan values it promotes is largely beside the point. What matters is whether portraying those values is a good business strategy. Disney is also a corporation that has received more than its share of criticism throughout its history. It has been criticised for its labour practices, for the cultural themes in its films, for the stands it takes (or does not take) on controversial public issues and, sometimes, simply for being a massive global corporation that strives to maximise its profits. This tension regularly leaves me puzzled. Is the value of my experience at Disney World undermined by the fact that it is, at the end of the day, a production of the Walt Disney Company? Can I trust a profit-hungry corporation to teach my children universal values? And does Disney’s message need to be sincere for it to really matter?

These sorts of questions are certainly not unique to Disney theme parks. In his book The Affluent Society (1958), the economist John Kenneth Galbraith coined the term ‘the dependence effect’ to characterise the process by which a business creates the desires that it seeks to satisfy. For example, you might not have wanted to buy a new sweater, but seeing a commercial on television makes you dissatisfied with your current wardrobe such that you hop online and order a new one. It likely never occurred to you to try iced tea with vodka until you saw the beverage advertised in a magazine, but now you find yourself on the way to the corner store to buy a six-pack. And Disney obviously wants to manufacture the desire to visit its theme parks because it will make money from everyone who wants to satisfy their newfound urge to ride Frozen Ever After and take pictures of their kids with Mickey and Minnie. For Galbraith, the dependence effect is problematic because it gives too much control over our lives to people who simply want to make money.

While contemporary critics of Disney might echo these concerns, the problem becomes more acute when the corporation in question has behaved poorly in other ways. The Walt Disney Company has long been the target of labour activists who criticise how Disney treats its employees. In 2024, unionised workers at Disneyland authorised a strike in contract negotiations where they argued that 73 per cent of their employees didn’t make enough money to cover basic living expenses, despite often working 12- to 14-hour days. That strike was ultimately averted, but it stands in a long line of labour controversies dating back to an animators’ strike in 1941, through protests about working conditions in the factories that produce Disney products, and most recently a series of layoffs across the company earlier this year.

There is a sense of something shared, however briefly and however manufactured, that I don’t find in many other places

Disney also has a decidedly mixed record on cultural issues. Writing in The Guardian in 2021, the journalist Steve Rose noted that:

Disney’s history of racist caricatures and ethnic stereotyping has been well documented and routinely criticised: the crows in Dumbo that drew on racist minstrel caricatures of African Americans; the Islamophobic tropes in Aladdin; the mockery of Native Americans in Peter Pan… the list goes on.

And its portrayals of women haven’t fared much better. As the media scholar Janet Wasko writes in her book Understanding Disney (2001):…

Why it is here: useful information, clear explanation

If you’ve ever struggled to stop doomscrolling before bed, impulse buying on your credit card or eating one too many sweets, you’ve probably noticed that simply knowing something is harmful doesn’t always translate into taking better actions. But as the US psychiatrist and educator Tracey Marks explains in this short video, we can leverage how our brains are wired to close that gap and break a bad habit. Marks starts by debunking common and unhelpful myths about what it takes to make a change – chief among them the idea that willpower alone is enough – before moving on to concrete strategies, like making the things that trigger a bad habit harder to access, and to how reframing our sense of identity can make new habits stick. For more on changing habits and cultivating healthier behaviours, read the Psyche Guide ‘How to resist everyday temptations’ (2025).

item.title: Meta pulls down controversial terms of service
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful information, clear explanation

Meta has indefinitely delayed its proposed commercial terms of service, which would have permitted the company to scrape the websites of Meta Business account users.

On Thursday, the company took down the preview link to the proposed terms and published an update to its Business Help Center that reads: “We recently shared that we were updating the Meta Commercial Terms, Product Catalog Terms, Self-Serve Ad Terms, and Ad Creative Generative AI Terms. These updates are now paused and will not take effect on November 20, 2026. We are continuing to consult with stakeholders and will provide a further update when we have more to share. In the meantime, our existing terms remain in effect.”

Meta confirmed the indefinite delay in a statement to Nieman Lab. “We’re pausing the changes as we continue to engage with stakeholders and take our time to get this right,” said a spokesperson for the company.

Meta — which owns Facebook, Messenger, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads — has repeatedly pushed back the terms’ effective date since Nieman Lab first reported on them on October 15. The terms were first set to take effect on October 30, sparking global outcry among news publishers, politicians, and trade organizations. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” On October 23, Meta moved the effective date back by three weeks to November 20.

Last week, Meta pledged to consult news publishers and industry leaders ahead of putting new commercial terms into effect.

“We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms update. We care deeply about our partners and do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted on October 28. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms.”

Since then, courts in Norway and Brazil have issued preliminary injunctions to block the terms from taking effect as a result of lawsuits filed by media organizations in both countries. The United Kingdom’s Competition and Markets Authority has opened a formal investigation into Meta, examining whether the company was “abusing a dominant position by imposing exploitative terms on publishers and advertisers.”

In the United States, the proposed terms stoked bipartisan concern. At the end of October, Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) sent letters to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg asking him to withdraw the terms.

item.title: With “Bimbo University,” Nikita Redkar leans into femininity to explain the news
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: interesting approach, clear explanation

The data is in: News creators and influencers are a major source of news for Americans, especially people under 30. This is the latest edition of Creators of Record, an occasional series of interviews with popular creators about how they do their jobs.

For Nikita Redkar, a big part of filming a video is putting together an outfit.

In a July video about youth-led protests in India, the 33-year-old is walking around New York City explaining how movements grow when people with opposing views come together on the things they do agree on. She’s wearing a white tube top and black jeans with sunglasses holding her hair back, along with a matching gold necklace and earrings that look like soda can tabs. You can’t see her shoes, but they clack enough for you to know she’s wearing a heel.

In another about comedian Shane Gillis’s Saturday Night Live monologue in which he called women “whores” for wearing shorts to the gym, she’s seated on the floor of her living room wearing a black silk velvet top with a pink faux-fur collar and sleeve cuffs. In the style of a Get Ready With Me video, she explains how 2000s comedy and pop culture entrenched misogynistic ideas of gender roles while applying her makeup.

A full-time news creator who mostly focuses on American politics and culture through a leftist and feminist lens, Redkar calls herself a “professor at Bimbo University.” The girliness is the point, she told me.

“I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice these parts of yourself to be taken seriously,” Redkar said. “You should be taken seriously no matter what.”

Four years into news content creation, Redkar has more than 943,000 TikTok followers, 674,000 Instagram followers, 33,000 YouTube subscribers, and 16,000 Substack subscribers. (Her handle on all of them is @nikitadumptruck.) She aims to explain issues in a way that’s funny and accessible — whether she’s attending protests outside the United Nations (“Get ready with me to bully Netanyahu”), traveling through Europe (“Spend the day in socialist hellhole Denmark with me”), or explaining the negative impacts of private equity companies (“A private equity boyfriend is this summer’s hottest accessory”).

Redkar and I chatted in October about how she does her job, leaning into her femininity to explain the news, and what her relationship with social media is like. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

In 2022, I had a video that really took off — like millions of views within a few hours. I was explaining the Russian invasion of Ukraine with a silly metaphor about Russia being a jealous ex that doesn’t want to see his ex thrive and be independent.

I tried that formula again a couple weeks later…about NATO and fears of World War III. I explained exactly what would be affected. I said there’s not going to be a world war, but things are going to get really expensive, which happened. I also used a girly friendship metaphor for that video. That’s when I started doing that formula — leaning into hyper-femininity to explain these complex geopolitical topics.

It’s important to make information accessible because we are going through so much news-wise and not all of it is easy to understand. I enjoy bringing this information I’m naturally interested in to people in a way where everyone [can] get involved.

It was really important to me to bring, colloquially speaking, the girls and the gays and the theys into the space, because it is fascinating and it provides context to what we’re going through right now. I feel like leftist content creators all operate on a spectrum. You have people who are getting really deep into Marxist theory, for example, and things like geopolitics. I’m at the beginning. But the reason I dial so deep into this hyper-femininity — leaning into these girly things like getting ready with me or walking with my outfit showing — is because I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice those parts of yourself to be taken seriously.
